title: International Klein Blue
hook: An artist found a way to keep blue pigment as bright on canvas as in the jar.
peek: Yves Klein loved the glowing blue of raw ultramarine powder, which turned dull once mixed into paint. With a Paris paint supplier he found a clear binder that kept the glow, registered the formula in 1960, and made it his signature.
lede: The French artist Yves Klein loved how loose ultramarine pigment glowed, and disliked how ordinary binders dulled it. Working with the Paris paint dealer Édouard Adam, he found a synthetic resin that held the powder in place while keeping its brightness. He registered the formula in 1960, and the result became International Klein Blue.

bullets.text: The secret was the binder, a clear synthetic resin sold as Rhodopas M60A, thinned with alcohol and other solvents. It holds the grains of pigment without drowning them, so the surface stays matt, powdery and intensely blue.

In a 1957 show in Milan, Klein hung eleven nearly identical blue paintings, each with a different price. He said buyers were paying for something beyond the object itself. From then on, blue became the colour most people link with his name.
Klein did not own the colour. In 1960 he filed a sealed record of the recipe with the French patent office, a way of proving the date of an idea rather than a patent that stops others using it.
In 1960 he staged performances where models covered in his blue pressed themselves onto large sheets of paper while musicians played. The prints became some of his best-known works.
